Berlin-based artist David Szauder recently shared a video that left me both mesmerised and unsettled. Seemingly inspired by the enigmatic frog deity Kek—an ancient Egyptian symbol of darkness, chaos, and the unseen forces that bring light—Szauder’s work feels like a poetic response to the seismic shifts rippling through the creative industries today.

View this post on Instagram
A post shared by David Szauder (@davidszauder)

The video unfolds like a fever dream—or perhaps a digital-age myth—as amorphous, chaotic forms dissolve, shift, and reassemble into fleeting moments of clarity, all set to the iconic hip-hop anthem Jump by House of Pain. Ancient symbolism collides with 21st-century disarray, crafting what feels like a mesmerising digital afterlife for the world of myth.
In ancient Egypt, frogs were more than nocturnal creatures—they symbolised transformation, heralding light from the depths of darkness. In Szauder’s animation, the frog is reimagined as a stand-in for the disruptive force of AI: unsettling, unpredictable, and, as the playful title HTYGF (How to Train Your Giant Frog) suggests, impossibly transformative.
What lingers, however, is not just the dazzling spectacle but the pressing questions it raises for the year ahead. Generative AI tools are rapidly challenging long-held workflows in 3D modelling and texturing. Where does this leave the artists and designers whose craft was built on manual precision and expertise? Are we witnessing the beginning of an unraveling—or the chaotic spark of an extraordinary creative renaissance?
Szauder doesn’t attempt to answer these questions outright. Like Kek, who straddled the line between light and shadow, destruction and creation, his work suggests that progress often emerges from disruption. The animation asks us to confront the generative potential of chaos and to reimagine a creative industry suspended between anxiety and possibility.
Watching his piece, I felt both excitement and unease. The frog myth has indeed leapt into the digital age, reminding us that, even in an AI-dominated landscape, the essence of creation still begins in the unknown.
As the lyrics echo in my mind:
“You’ve got to get out your seat and jump around, Disruption’s the beat, so don’t stand your ground.“
What’s your take? Is this a leap toward a brighter creative future—or a harbinger of chaos that challenges the very foundations of artistry?

On 60 Minutes, Bill Whitaker asked Giacomo Massari of LITIX (a company using robots to carve marble sculptures) what many are thinking:

“If you have a robot doing 99% of the work, where’s the artistry?”

Massari didn’t blink:

“In the idea, how you program the machine. It’s a work of art because it’s an artistic approach. You need to have a sculptural background to program the machine in the way that you want.”

Translation: the chisel is code. The artist is still here. She just speaks Python.
This is the new creative battleground. As AI and automation steamroll into traditionally “human” domains, we have two choices: evolve, or complain from the cheap seats. The future of creativity isn’t about resisting the machine. It’s about learning how to direct it.
We’re not being replaced by AI. We’re being replaced by people who know how to work with it.

During this time of saturation in American media coverage, especially surrounding the U.S. election, the Dor Brothers have been at it again! Their latest mind-bending project, “Lies Wide Shut”, delves into the murky waters of media manipulation and simulation, echoing Jean Baudrillard’s Simulacra and Simulation, where the boundary between the real and the simulated becomes increasingly blurred. In true Baudrillardian style, the project leaves us questioning what’s true and what’s merely an artfully constructed illusion.
In Simulacra, Baudrillard famously uses Disneyland as an example of a place that functions as a fantasy while suggesting that the rest of the world has become equally hyperreal. This draws attention to the larger simulation we live in:

“Disneyland est là pour masquer que c’est le pays ‘réel’, toute l’Amérique ‘réelle’, qui est Disneyland… Disneyland est présenté comme imaginaire afin de faire croire que le reste est réel, alors que… l’Amérique qui l’entoure… appartient à l’ordre de l’hyperréel et de la simulation.”
(Translation: “Disneyland is presented as imaginary in order to make us believe that the rest is real, when in fact all of Los Angeles and the America surrounding it are no longer real, but of the order of the hyperreal and of simulation.”) — Baudrillard, J. (1981). Simulacres et simulation. Éditions Galilée.

The title “Lies Wide Shut”, a clear nod to Stanley Kubrick’s Eyes Wide Shut, suggests a deliberate focus on exposing hidden truths that lie beneath the surface of widely accepted societal narratives. This sets the tone for the Dor Brothers’ sharp investigation into the artificiality embedded in our media-saturated world, where carefully curated simulations often mask deeper, uncomfortable realities.

“What is a number, that a man may know it, and a man that he may know a number.”

In this rare 1962 interview filmed in Old Lyme, Connecticut, Warren McCulloch—barefoot, shirtless, and full of energy—feels like a mix of Aldous Huxley, George Orwell, and the actor Willem Dafoe, with his wild, piercing gaze. The conversation offers a glimpse into the mind of one of the early thinkers in artificial intelligence.
McCulloch’s work laid the foundation for many of the AI technologies that shape our world today, from neural networks and natural language processing to the swift advancements in generative AI.

His spooky words, “Don’t shake the table…” as the interview closes, echo with a certain finality—an early and important call for ethical consideration as AI progresses.

1. Executive Snapshot

Role: Behavioural Researcher & Strategic Design Lead
Duration: Multi-phase community intervention
Context: Informal settlement households using unsafe flame-based cooking systems

Core Problem: Low adoption of safer cookstove technologies despite significant health and safety risks.
Outcome: Designed and implemented a community-based behavioural intervention using bread-baking as a participatory catalyst, contributing to measurable shifts in cookstove ownership patterns and safety perceptions.
2. Strategic Context
In many low-resource South African communities, households rely on open-flame cooking systems, paraffin, and biomass fuels, often within structurally unsafe stoves.
Consequences include: - Respiratory illness and indoor air pollution - Burn injuries - Fuel inefficiency and financial strain
Despite the availability of safer alternatives, adoption rates remained low because barriers were not purely economic—they were behavioural, cultural, and identity-linked. The challenge was shifted from a product distribution problem to a behavioural systems challenge: shifting motivations and norms without imposing external solutions.
3. Research & Diagnostic Phase
Research Questions

What symbolic and cultural meanings are attached to cooking with fire?
What prevents households from transitioning to safer cookstoves?
Which social influences shape ownership decisions?
How do risk perceptions align with daily lived realities?

Methods

Ethnographic fieldwork and in-home observations
Semi-structured interviews and behavioural mapping
Co-creation workshops and informal community discussions
Artefact analysis of existing stove types and usage patterns

Constraints

Financial vulnerability and infrastructure instability
Deep-rooted cooking traditions
Trust barriers toward external interventions


Key Diagnostic Insight: The cookstove was not merely a utility device; it represented identity, competence, and family provision. Therefore, messaging focused solely on “health risks” failed to motivate change.

4. Key Behavioural Insights

Normalisation of Risk: Health dangers were acknowledged but behaviourally discounted.
Social Proof Dominance: Adoption decisions were strongly influenced by visible community norms.
Capability and Pride: Participants responded better to narratives of capability and pride than to fear.
Demonstration Over Instruction: Hands-on experience produced stronger engagement than informational campaigns.

5. Intervention Design
The curriculum was structured around three behavioural pillars:

Predatory Pricing Allegations and Dairy Industry Consolidation: Reassessing Parmalat’s Role in Global Dairy Markets
Abstract
The expansion of multinational dairy processors such as Parmalat, later integrated into the Lactalis Group, has generated allegations of aggressive pricing strategies designed to capture market share from smaller dairies and milk producers, followed by potential recoupment through elevated prices. This synthesis critically evaluates the available evidence across key jurisdictions, particularly South Africa and Australia, within the broader context of agri-food industry consolidation. Drawing on competition authority reports, stakeholder submissions, policy analyses, and peer-reviewed literature in industrial organization and agricultural economics, the review finds that claims of classic predatory pricing—sustained below-cost sales with demonstrable recoupment potential—remain weakly supported and largely unproven under established antitrust standards [1].
In South Africa, Parmalat’s 1998 market entry was associated with a reported price war and downward pressure on raw milk producer prices, with one policy report citing an approximate 28% reduction [2]. However, this evidence is primarily anecdotal and does not include the cost-based or recoupment analyses required to establish predation. In Australia, intense retail discounting (“milk wars”) transmitted price pressure to processors including Parmalat, prompting farmer characterizations of the conduct as predatory; yet the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) determined that such discounting did not constitute predatory pricing and reflected normal competitive dynamics [3], [4].
Available documentation more robustly indicates exercises of buyer (monopsonistic) power over fragmented farmers, occasional horizontal coordination among processors, and structural consolidation driven by retail concentration and scale economies [5], [6]. Methodological limitations—reliance on qualitative testimony, absence of firm-specific variable cost data, and challenges in isolating Parmalat’s conduct from supermarket-led strategies—preclude strong causal attribution to deliberate monopolization via predation. The synthesis concludes that while Parmalat’s operations coincided with accelerated small-producer exits, the evidence better supports broader patterns of buyer power and industry consolidation than legally cognizable predatory pricing. Theoretical implications for antitrust enforcement in agricultural chains and directions for future empirical research are discussed. (242 words)
Introduction
Global dairy processing exhibits pronounced economies of scale, perishability constraints, and dual-sided market power: concentrated retailers upstream and fragmented agricultural producers downstream. Against this backdrop, Parmalat’s international expansion raised concerns regarding potential abuse of dominance through below-cost pricing aimed at eliminating smaller competitors. This synthesis examines whether empirical and documentary sources substantiate allegations of predatory pricing by Parmalat across multiple markets, defined under strategic theory as pricing below an appropriate cost measure (typically average variable cost) with a dangerous probability of recouping losses after rival exit [1].
The analysis adopts an industrial organization lens, distinguishing predatory pricing from related but distinct phenomena: monopsonistic buyer power, horizontal collusion on input prices, and retailer-driven loss-leading. Scope encompasses publicly available materials on South Africa, Australia, and select European contexts, with emphasis on post-liberalization periods. By synthesizing regulatory determinations, stakeholder accounts, and peer-reviewed scholarship, this review highlights evidentiary gaps and situates Parmalat’s conduct within structural transformations of modern agricultural markets [5].
Critical Analysis & Synthesis
Theoretical Framework: Predatory Pricing versus Buyer Power
Predatory pricing doctrine requires demonstration of below-cost pricing, anticompetitive intent or effect (rival exclusion), and recoupment feasibility [1]. In agri-food chains, however, observed price pressures more frequently reflect buyer power, whereby processors or retailers leverage bargaining asymmetry against numerous small suppliers to depress input (farmgate) prices without necessarily engaging in below-cost output sales [5], [6]. Sexton (2013) emphasizes that modern agricultural markets often feature thin trading, asymmetric information, and high search costs, facilitating coordination or unilateral exercises of market power that differ markedly from classic predation models.

[1] P. Bolton, J. F. Brodley, and M. H. Riordan, ‘Predatory pricing: Strategic theory and legal policy’, Georgetown Law Journal, vol. 88, pp. 2239–2330, 2000.
South African Market Entry and Price Dynamics
Parmalat’s entry into South Africa in 1998 reportedly triggered a price war, with products offered to retailers at reduced rates followed by pressure on producers, resulting in an approximate 28% decline in milk producer prices according to one labor and economic research institute report [2]. This account frames the episode as contributing to sector instability and disproportionate impacts on smaller distributors. Nevertheless, the source constitutes policy advocacy rather than a rigorous empirical study; it lacks detailed cost reconstructions or recoupment analysis. Subsequent investigations by South African authorities more commonly addressed alleged horizontal coordination on raw milk surpluses and pricing among processors, including Parmalat, rather than vertical predation in consumer markets. Such findings align with monopsony concerns over input suppression rather than monopoly power in final goods [5].

[2] Institute for Labour and Economic Research, ‘Restructuring of the dairy industry: What impact?’, ILRIG South Africa, 2020. Available: https://www.ilrigsa.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/restructuring-the-dairy-screen.pdf
Australian Retail-Driven Price Wars and Processor Transmission
In Australia, the 2011 “milk wars” initiated by supermarket private-label discounting generated substantial farmgate price volatility. Farmer submissions to Senate inquiries characterized processor responses—including those involving Parmalat—as patterns likely to eliminate branded products and smaller players, invoking the term “predatory pricing” [4]. The ACCC, however, explicitly found that Coles’ house-brand discounting did not breach competition law or constitute predatory pricing, citing legitimate competitive purposes and insufficient evidence of long-term anticompetitive harm [3]. Processor margins were squeezed as retail bargaining power transmitted lower wholesale prices downstream, illustrating vertical pass-through of buyer power rather than unilateral processor predation. This dynamic underscores the analytical importance of distinguishing supermarket loss-leading from processor strategies [6].

[4] A. P. H. S. E. R. Committee, ‘Impacts of supermarket price decisions on the dairy industry’. 2011.

[3] Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, ‘Dairy inquiry’, ACCC, 2017.

[6] Z. Chen, ‘Buyer power in the theory of industrial organization’, Review of Industrial Organization, 2003, doi: 10.1023/A:1027385122198.
Horizontal Coordination and European Contexts
Evidence of Parmalat/Lactalis involvement appears stronger in horizontal matters, such as alleged coordination on raw milk acquisition in South Africa and information exchange or collusion cases in Spain concerning raw milk supply. These episodes concern buyer-side practices aimed at input price stabilization or suppression, not below-cost consumer sales followed by output price elevation. Such patterns reinforce the monopsony framework articulated in the literature, where processor concentration enables collective influence over fragmented suppliers without satisfying predatory pricing criteria [5].
Structural Drivers of Consolidation
Across jurisdictions, small dairy exits reflect multifaceted pressures: retail concentration, technological advantages (e.g., UHT processing), global commodity volatility, and scale economies favoring large multinationals. Peer-reviewed analyses caution against attributing consolidation predominantly to single-firm predation when systemic factors predominate [5]. The absence of granular, firm-level cost data and longitudinal pricing-recoupment studies across sources limits causal inference regarding Parmalat’s specific role.

[5] R. J. Sexton, ‘Market power, misconceptions, and modern agricultural markets’, American Journal of Agricultural Economics, vol. 95, no. 2, pp. 209–219, 2013, doi: 10.1093/ajae/aat035.
Discussion
Significant limitations constrain the current evidentiary base. Most materials rely on stakeholder testimony or aggregate trends rather than econometric tests of predation (e.g., difference-in-differences around entry events or margin reconstructions). Distinguishing Parmalat’s conduct from retailer dominance and industry-wide liberalization effects remains challenging. Post-2003 accounting scandal restructuring and Lactalis integration further complicate longitudinal assessment. Future research should prioritize DOI-indexed econometric studies employing administrative cost-price datasets to test recoupment hypotheses more rigorously and compare dairy sub-sectors (fresh pasteurized vs. UHT).
These findings carry policy significance for antitrust in agri-food sectors, where conventional predation standards may undervalue cumulative buyer-power effects. Enhanced supplier protections, such as enforceable dairy codes, warrant consideration alongside preservation of consumer benefits from competitive pricing.
Conclusion
Available sources provide limited corroboration for systematic predatory pricing by Parmalat involving sustained below-cost sales, targeted elimination of small dairies, and subsequent monopoly recoupment. Instead, the record more strongly supports patterns of aggressive competition, monopsonistic pressures on producers, retailer-driven discounting, and structural consolidation in dairy markets. Reframing analysis around buyer power and industry dynamics, rather than classic predation, yields a more defensible and nuanced understanding of Parmalat’s role. Rigorous empirical scholarship remains essential to inform competition policy in global agri-food chains.

Meet Wally & Dave

Meet Wally and Dave.
The hilarious Richard Pryor plays Wally. Wally is competely blind. Yet he pretends that he can see. So he has built up a system around him of memorised cues and contextual guesses. He reads newspapers he cannot see. Navigates the world on muscle memory and sheer guile. Which is not the same thing as being able to see. [pause]
Gene Wilder plays Wally’s partner Dave. Dave is deaf. Like Wally, he has become very good at pretending that he can hear. He lip-reads. He guesses. He fills the silence with whatever his training gives him — and delivers the result with complete conviction. [pause]
Together, they are unstoppable. Wally strides forward. Dave shouts what he thinks he lip-read. Each one borrows the faculty the other is performing. Neither of them actually has it. What makes it funny is that everyone around them can see exactly what’s happening. Everyone except them. [click]

This gap in perception seems to be a human failure, not a technical one. We blindly feed the AI models expecting miraculous responses. We first need to bring the spatial reality and lived experience into the room. The AI cannot know what it hasn’t been given. It confidently performs based on learned patterns like Wally. We’ve confused well-structured prompts with insight, creating solutions that are technically coherent but humanly wrong. We have handed our eyes to something blind.

It’s Dave shouting directions. And Wally striding forward like he owns the place. [smiling]

The Deaf Leading the Blind: What Silicon Valley’s LLMs Cannot See

“…They have mouths, but cannot speak, eyes, but cannot see. They have ears, but cannot hear, noses, but cannot smell… Those who make them will be like them, and so will all who trust in them.” (Psalm 115:4–8, NIV)

I recently found myself watching See No Evil, Hear No Evil — a minor 1989 comedy — on YouTube, drawn in by the “I am white” clip with Richard Pryor (Figure 1). The hilarious Pryor plays Wally, a blind man who flatly refuses to admit it. Gene Wilder plays Dave, a deaf man who has become remarkably good at pretending to hear (Figure 2). Together they blunder through a murder mystery, each borrowing the faculty of the other. Wally strides into bar brawls while Dave shouts directions (Figure 3). Dave borrows Wally’s ears to detect approaching sirens. The comedy turns on the gap between performed and actual perception. On reflection, it could be a surprisingly accurate description of artificial intelligence (AI), specifically visual-focussed Large Language Models (LLMs).







Figure 1: In this subway sequence, Wally (Pryor) performs “simulated sight”, using memorised cues to mask his blindness.








Figure 2: During the job interview, Wally and Dave attempt to communicate across a complete sensory disconnect.








Figure 3: Wally and Dave in a bar brawl.




Silicon Valley has spent the better part of a decade equipping AI with eyes. Visual encoders. Camera inputs. The image-upload button is presented to us with confidence that the machine can now see. What the product announcements rarely discuss is the architecture sitting behind the lens. The LLMs process visual information by first converting it into words, then reasoning about those words, and finally describing what they believe to be there. All with the practised confidence of a man who cannot see the bar fight he has just walked into.
The Wally Problem
Silicon Valley’s flagship general-purpose LLMs still have the language bottleneck firmly in place. The system works, ostensibly, because this partnership is all it has. This is, in essence, a Wally problem. Vision for most multimodal AI systems relies on a process of narration, not perception. Pixels enter; the language model converts them into tokens; the tokens are then reasoned about (Su et al., 2025). Under light cognitive load, this works well enough. Under heavier demands requiring genuine inference, the visual attention collapses, and the model does what researchers have delicately termed “relying on linguistic priors” (Qian et al., 2026). It does a Wally. It narrates the world it expects rather than the one in front of it. In other words, it does not merely struggle to see. It hallucinates with pre-trained confidence.

Qian, Z., Ma, Y., Ouyang, Z., Wang, Z., Xu, Z., Luo, F., Liu, X., Ge, Z., Guo, Y., & Han, J. (2026). Cognitive pivot points and visual anchoring: Unveiling and rectifying hallucinations in multimodal reasoning models. arXiv Preprint arXiv:2604.10219. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10219
But What About Tesla?
An instinctive counter-argument is Tesla. If the LLM cannot see, how then is a two-tonne vehicle able to negotiate Californian roads without incident? The answer is not that Tesla has solved the vision problem. The Tesla v12 architecture maps pixels directly to steering and braking outputs, bypassing language altogether. There is no Dave whispering directions to Wally here. The blind man has simply been removed. The car does not name a stop sign before responding to it; it encodes the sign as a spatial object with associated coordinates and probabilities, and acts accordingly.
And Midjourney?
Another apparent counter-argument is the proliferation of visual generation tools, of which Midjourney is the prime example. The remarkable images these models produce seem to have mastered the disconnect. The light behaves. The geometry holds. The shadows fall where shadows ought to fall. One is almost persuaded. One is reminded of Wally discovering, late in the film, that he has become a rather convincing actor. Which is not the same thing as having recovered his sight. What Midjourney has mastered is the aesthetics of plausibility (Su et al., 2025). Through heroic quantities of human feedback, it has learned the statistical grammar of what beautiful images look like. It has learnt the precise pixel distribution that human evaluators label as “a convincing glass of wine” or “a plausible city at night”. It does not know that glass shatters, nor that wine is liquid. It is navigating a latent mapping of human visual taste.

Zhou, Y., Wang, Y., He, X., Xiao, R., Li, Z., Feng, Q., Guo, Z., Yang, Y., Wu, H., Huang, W., Wei, J., Si, D., Yao, X., Bu, J., Huang, H., Fu, T., Tang, S., Fei, B., Zhou, D., … Bai, L. (2025). Scientists’ first exam: Probing cognitive abilities of MLLM via perception, understanding, and reasoning. arXiv Preprint arXiv:2506.10521. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10521
The results are often beautiful, yet in the scientific domain — where spatial truth is crucial — they are completely unpredictable. When researchers recently evaluated leading multimodal models on scientific tasks requiring perception, interpretation, and reasoning over real data, performance was strikingly limited. The models achieved only around 30% accuracy, revealing substantial gaps in their ability to integrate visual information with scientific reasoning (Zhou et al., 2025).
The perception may be absent, but the vocabulary remains intact. Wally, as it turns out, knows all the right words for a bar fight.
These failures are not just academic. They are alarming. Engineers developing collaborative tools for blind and low-vision users have discovered that AI-mediated visual description collapses on the very information those users most need: spatial structure (Li et al., 2026). Where is the annotation relative to the diagram? Which cluster corresponds to which label? The visual grammar of arrangement — proximity as semantic signal — evaporates in translation. A system that cannot genuinely parse space cannot reconstruct it for the people whose relationship to space is already precarious. Asking Wally to give directions, in other words, has consequences that extend well beyond comedy.

Li, M., Yang, H., Sanda, N., & Das, M. (2026). Idea11y: Enhancing accessibility in collaborative ideation for blind or low vision screen reader users. Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3790878

Su, Z., Xia, P., Guo, H., Liu, Z., Ma, Y., Qu, X., Liu, J., Li, Y., Zeng, K., Yang, Z., Li, L., Cheng, Y., Ji, H., He, J., & Fung, Y. R. (2025). Thinking with images for multimodal reasoning: Foundations, methods, and future frontiers. arXiv Preprint arXiv:2506.23918. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23918
The field is not entirely unaware of the predicament. A growing body of research advocates for what its proponents call “thinking with images” rather than thinking about them — reasoning natively in visual latent space rather than routing every observation through the linguistic bottleneck first (Su et al., 2025). Whether this amounts to a genuine architectural reckoning or a more sophisticated performance of sight is, for now, an open question.
The partnership of Wally and Dave, for the moment, endures. Wally strides forward; Dave shouts what he thinks he lip-reads. The demos are polished. The press releases are stirring. The benchmarks, carefully selected, are excellent.
The bar fight, however, is still going on. And it is becoming increasingly difficult for us, as outsiders, to tell which punches are actually landing and which ones are merely striking empty air.

The Spotted Ape
How the work fits together
Strategy identifies the choices an organisation must make. Learning develops the capability to act on them. Judgement tests whether the choices and their consequences remain sound.



01 / Strategy as choice
A strategy connects choices about where to compete and how to create an advantage.
In the approach described by A.G. Lafley and Roger Martin in Playing to Win, strategy connects choices about ambition, competitive focus, advantage, capabilities and supporting management systems. Their Strategy Choice Cascade helps teams examine whether these choices support one another.
The Strategy Choice Cascade matters because its choices constrain and reinforce one another. A new ambition without a choice of arena is difficult to act on. An arena without a distinctive way to win can become a market description. A proposed advantage without the capability and operating conditions to sustain it remains an assertion.
We help teams make these links visible, including the choices they will not pursue. Analysis informs the choices; it does not remove the responsibility to make them.
Explore the Strategic Decision Workshop




02 / Design and inquiry
Use evidence to make uncertainty workable.
Strategic questions rarely arrive as problems with a single known answer. Design thinking helps teams move between understanding a situation, framing a consequential problem, generating alternatives and learning from tests. It keeps attention on the people, systems and conditions that shape whether a choice can work.
Deductive reasoning asks what follows from stated premises. Inductive reasoning looks for patterns in observations. Abductive reasoning asks what might explain what is happening, or what could plausibly work. It creates hypotheses, not proof. For a proposed strategy, the team identifies the conditions it requires and the evidence that would challenge those conditions. This strategic inquiry draws on Roger Martin’s question, “What would have to be true?”.
The practical aim is not endless ideation. It is to turn uncertain assumptions into questions that can change a decision.




03 / Organisational learning
Knowledge must travel into practice.
Documents, procedures and repositories preserve knowledge. They are useful stocks, but a stock is not the same as the ability to apply, adapt or question what is stored. Some important knowledge is tacit: people develop it through participation, observation, adjustment and work with others.
Learning therefore depends on flows as well as storage. Who can reach whom? Where can a practitioner show how a decision is made? What recurring work allows another person to try, receive feedback and improve? What happens when an experiment reveals that an established assumption no longer fits?
Communities of practice and creation spaces can make such exchange possible. They need a real problem, access to relevant people and resources, room to make and test, and a path back to decisions and operating practice. They are not simply new names for training rooms or repositories.
Explore the Knowledge Sharing & Organisational Learning Lab




04 / Knowing, making, playing
A different way to learn can reveal a different problem.
John Seely Brown’s account of learning makes room for three complementary modes. Knowing brings concepts, evidence and experience into view. Making gives an idea a form that can be examined. Playing makes it possible to try a variation, change perspective and reframe the question.
In a strategy setting, a team might first describe what it believes about customers and competition; sketch a different way to create value; then use a scenario to test how a customer, competitor or colleague might respond. The sketch is not a forecast. It is a concrete hypothesis the team can discuss, revise or set aside.
This sequence can open a new problem space without treating play as an end in itself. Each activity should inform a strategic question or a capability the organisation needs to develop.
Explore the Strategy Prototyping Studio




05 / Designed executive learning
The learning design is part of the intervention.
Before selecting activities, we need to understand who is in the room, what they already know, which decisions they can influence and what they need to do afterwards. Learning outcomes should be specific enough to guide both the session and its tangible outputs.
We distinguish three kinds of outcome:


Knowledge
What participants need to understand: a strategic concept, the evidence available, or the structure of a decision.


Skills
What participants need to practise: mapping choices, articulating assumptions, prototyping a scenario or tracing knowledge through work.


Wisdom
What participants need to judge: which evidence is sufficient, what uncertainty to accept, what to test next and who remains accountable.


The format follows the outcome. A short explanation can introduce a concept; participants then apply it to a live or representative problem. A scenario can ask them to judge a choice from another stakeholder’s position. Discussion and critique make reasoning visible. Breaks and changes of activity are planned around the audience and the work, not a claimed universal minute-by-minute rule.
Participants should leave with a useful working artefact: for example, a record of strategic choices structured using the Strategy Choice Cascade, a hypothesis-and-test map, a knowledge-flow blueprint, a scenario prototype or explicit decision rights. It is a basis for further work, not a guarantee that an organisation will implement it.




06 / From choice to action
One connected working sequence.


Frame the decisionAgree the organisational question, participants, evidence and boundaries.


Make choices explicitUse the Strategy Choice Cascade to connect ambition, competitive focus, advantage, capabilities and supporting management practices.


Surface assumptionsIdentify the conditions each option requires and the evidence that would change the team’s view.


Make and testUse a scenario, prototype or work-based activity to examine a hypothesis.


Design for learningIdentify the knowledge, practice and relationships needed to develop capability.


Decide and reviewRecord the choice, unresolved questions, owners and a proportionate next test.


The sequence is adapted to the work. A team may return to an earlier choice when new evidence changes the problem; the sequence is a guide for inquiry, not a maturity scale.




Judgement and responsibility
Tools can contribute. People still own consequential choices.
AI can alter how quickly teams generate options, analyse information and produce work. That makes the purpose, evidence threshold, decision rights and learning consequences more important to specify. Where a system recommends or acts, a useful design asks who can inspect it, challenge it, stop it and remain accountable for the outcome.
This concern connects the strategic and learning work to The Spotted Ape’s existing interest in human judgement, agency and organisational integrity. It is relevant where AI is changing work, but it does not require every strategy or learning problem to be framed as an AI problem.
Our strategy work draws on the Strategy Choice Cascade described in Playing to Win by A.G. Lafley and Roger Martin. Our learning design also draws on John Seely Brown and Fitzpatrick & Hunt. Our contribution is to combine established strategic approaches with behavioural design, practical learning and human judgement, applying them to the organisation’s decisions and working conditions. These are intellectual foundations, not partnerships, endorsements or proprietary frameworks of The Spotted Ape.

The Spotted Ape
Where are teams stuck?
The same visible symptom can have different causes. Use these questions to find a useful starting point, not to score or diagnose your organisation.



Find a starting point
What is getting in the way?


The Planning Trap
There is a plan, but leaders have not agreed where to compete, why customers will choose the organisation, or what it will stop doing.
Explore the challenge


Analytical Paralysis
The evidence keeps growing while the choice, the assumptions and the next test remain unclear.
Explore the challenge


Knowledge That Does Not Reach the Work
Important knowledge sits in documents and repositories, while teams struggle to use it in changing work.
Explore the challenge


Tacit Knowledge Silos
Experienced practitioners know how the work gets done, but that knowledge is difficult to share or learn through practice.
Explore the challenge


The Innovation Disconnect
Promising ideas and experiments do not connect to strategic choices, operational capability or a next decision.
Explore the challenge


Executive Alignment
Leaders agree on aspirations but hold different assumptions about customers, competition, trade-offs or capabilities.
Explore the challenge






01 / Strategic choice
The Planning Trap
What it can look like
Planning documents describe targets, initiatives and resource allocations, but the leadership team cannot explain the connected choices intended to create a competitive advantage. Priorities accumulate; explicit exclusions do not.
Why it persists
Planning is often easier to coordinate around what the organisation controls than around uncertain customer response and competitive reaction. Analysis can refine assumptions without requiring anyone to make a trade-off.
The underlying issue
The organisation may have a plan without an integrated strategy: connected choices about ambition, competitive focus, advantage, the capabilities required and the management practices that support them.
A useful intervention
The Strategic Decision Workshop uses the Strategy Choice Cascade described by A.G. Lafley and Roger Martin in Playing to Win to connect the team’s choices, clarify exclusions and identify assumptions to test.
Explore the Strategic Decision Workshop




02 / Assumption testing
Analytical Paralysis
What it can look like
Teams commission more research, compare another set of options and defer commitment because no available analysis appears to remove uncertainty.
Why it persists
Evidence can narrow a question, but it cannot choose the organisation’s goals or eliminate uncertainty about the future. Without a decision rule, another plausible alternative can always reopen the discussion.
The underlying issue
The team may lack a working hypothesis and a clear account of what evidence would change its mind. Deductive and inductive analysis matter, but so does abductive reasoning: asking what might be true, then testing it.
A useful intervention
The Strategy Prototyping Studio helps teams create alternatives, identify the conditions each alternative requires, and design bounded scenarios or experiments that can inform a choice.
Explore the Strategy Prototyping Studio




03 / Knowledge flows
Knowledge That Does Not Reach the Work
What it can look like
The organisation has manuals, reports and training materials, yet teams cannot reliably bring relevant knowledge into a new customer problem, changed process or unfamiliar situation.
Why it persists
Repositories preserve explicit information, but access alone does not create the context, relationships or practice needed to apply it. As conditions change, stored answers can become less useful without a way to interpret and revise them.
The underlying issue
Knowledge is treated mainly as a stock to store and distribute, rather than also as a flow created through work, exchange, feedback and adaptation.
A useful intervention
The Knowledge Sharing & Organisational Learning Lab maps where useful knowledge resides, how it moves between people and work, and where teams can learn by making and testing in a bounded setting.
Explore the Knowledge Sharing & Organisational Learning Lab




04 / Tacit practice
Tacit Knowledge Silos
What it can look like
Work depends on the judgement of a few experienced practitioners. Their expertise is difficult to express as instructions, new colleagues have limited opportunities to observe it, and teams repeat avoidable discovery.
Why it persists
Much practical knowledge is situated: people notice cues, make adjustments and coordinate with others in ways they may not be able to explain in a document. Conventional training can describe a practice without recreating the conditions in which it is learned.
The underlying issue
The organisation has not designed enough opportunities for observation, participation, peer exchange and reflection around real work.
A useful intervention
The Knowledge Sharing & Organisational Learning Lab identifies practitioners, relationships and recurring work where knowledge can move through communities of practice, shared tasks and creation spaces.
Explore the Knowledge Sharing & Organisational Learning Lab




05 / Experimentation
The Innovation Disconnect
What it can look like
Teams generate concepts and run pilots, but promising activity does not change a strategic choice, build a capability or establish what the organisation should test next.
Why it persists
Exploration can become detached from the decisions it is meant to inform. Conversely, an existing strategy can constrain experiments to small improvements that never test whether the original assumptions still hold.
The underlying issue
The learning loop is incomplete: a hypothesis is not connected to a meaningful strategic question, and results do not lead to a decision to continue, adapt or stop.
A useful intervention
The Strategy Prototyping Studio connects knowing, making and playful reframing. Teams prototype plausible futures, surface assumptions and agree what an experiment could help them learn.
Explore the Strategy Prototyping Studio




06 / Shared choices
Executive Alignment
What it can look like
Leaders express similar ambitions but disagree in practice about which customers matter, how the organisation will compete, which capabilities to develop or what risks it will accept.
Why it persists
Broad goals can conceal incompatible assumptions. A meeting may record agreement without exposing the trade-offs or clarifying who owns the decision and the next test.
The underlying issue
Alignment is treated as consensus on language rather than a shared, revisable set of choices and an understanding of what those choices require.
A useful intervention
An Executive Offsite or the Strategic Decision Workshop makes differences in assumptions visible, tests critical hypotheses and records the choices, open questions and owners that follow.
Discuss an executive session




Scope before solution
A starting point, not a diagnosis.
These patterns can overlap and have different causes in different organisations. An initial conversation helps establish the decision or work system involved, who needs to participate and whether a workshop is a sensible next step.

The Spotted Ape
The !Khairos Capability Progression
Professional capability must remain viable as the conditions of work change.



The organising question
What remains yours to do?
An Agentic Designer shapes a system in which people and machines possess forms of agency. Designing that relationship means more than allocating tasks.
What are we trying to achieve? What may the machine recommend or execute? What should neither a person nor a machine be allowed to do automatically? What evidence is required, who can override the result and what happens when confidence is low?
It also means asking how expertise develops. A task can be efficient to delegate and valuable to practise. The choice depends on its purpose, consequences and the people learning through it.
!Khairos connects behavioural science’s attention to how people decide, strategic design’s concern with purpose and context, and systems thinking’s attention to feedback and consequences.




Five stages
A change in role, made visible in practice.

01 / Assisted
Explorer
Shift — From accepting plausible production to inspecting how a judgement was reached.
Practice — Compare an output with the brief. Mark evidence, inference, unsupported claims and missing information before accepting it.
Intended artefact — An initial Human Agency Map and an annotated work sample.
Reflection — Where did fluent wording or confidence stand in for a reason to trust the answer?


02 / Structured
Practitioner
Shift — From improvising with a tool to setting criteria and constraints.
Practice — State purpose, audience, evidence threshold and a stopping rule. Apply the same rubric to alternatives and explain exclusions.
Intended artefact — A Judgement Rubric adapted to a recurring task.
Reflection — Did I choose the criteria first, or invent them to defend the answer I already preferred?


03 / Orchestrated
Integrator
Shift — From judging an isolated output to designing how work passes between people and machines.
Practice — Map decisions, verification, hand-offs and feedback. Test whether each human intervention is possible and meaningful.
Intended artefact — An Agentic Workflow Blueprint.
Reflection — Where did a convenient default become a decision? Whose attention or learning does the workflow depend on?


04 / Agentic
Architect
Shift — From using a workflow to specifying conditional machine agency.
Practice — Define what may be recommended or executed, the required evidence, override rights and conditions for stopping or escalation. Rehearse a failure.
Intended artefact — A Decision Rights Map linked to the blueprint.
Reflection — Am I delegating a task, a judgement or responsibility? Would someone else recognise the distinction?


05 / Governed
Steward — Governed autonomy
Shift — From specifying the system to remaining responsible for its outcomes and its effects on capability.
Practice — Review decisions and consequences over time. Revise boundaries, escalation and learning practices when the evidence warrants it.
Intended artefact — Revised maps and rubric, with a record of decisions, exceptions and review.
Reflection — What is the team no longer practising? Are our incentives making meaningful scrutiny harder?





Formation over time
Practice → critique → reflection → revision.
The framework is used to design repeated learning, not to award a rank. Participants bring work and its reasoning, test it with peers and reviewers, then revise their criteria or workflow in the next task.
A team may need close human scrutiny in one workflow and conditional autonomy in another. Moving backwards to re-examine a weak criterion can be more mature than adding another automated action.
Governance follows from agency: once a system can act, decision rights, boundaries and consequences must be explicit. At Steward level, review includes the capabilities the team is retaining or losing.
How the capability programme uses this progression





Southern African provenance
Form that holds under constraint.
Welwitschia mirabilis provides the framework’s Namib Desert point of reference. The earlier site described its resilience through the meeting of “wet and dry”: a form that persists without waiting for the environment to become easier.
The professional parallel is a capability organised to remain viable when conditions change. A particular tool, interface or production routine may disappear. The capacity to frame a purpose, judge evidence, recognise uncertainty and take responsibility still needs a structure in which to develop.
This is a restrained design metaphor, not a biological theory of organisations. It directs attention towards what makes a practice durable: constraints, feedback, deliberate intervention and learning. The progression is a working framework, not an independently validated measurement scale.

The Deaf Leading the Blind: What Silicon Valley’s LLM’s Cannot See

“…They have mouths, but cannot speak, eyes, but cannot see. They have ears, but cannot hear, noses, but cannot smell… Those who make them will be like them, and so will all who trust in them.” (Psalm 115:4–8, NIV)

I recently found myself watching See No Evil, Hear No Evil on Youtube, drawn in by the “I am white” clip with Richard Pryor (Figure 1). It is a minor 1989 comedy. The hilarious Pryor plays Wally, a blind man who refuses to acknowledge that he is blind. Gene Wilder plays Dave, a deaf man who has become remarkably good at pretending to hear. Together they blunder through a murder mystery, each borrowing the faculty of the other. Wally strides into bar brawls while Dave shouts directions. Dave borrows Wally’s ears to detect approaching sirens. The comedy turns on the gap between performed and actual perception (Figure 2). On reflection, it could be a surprisingly accurate description of artificial intelligence (AI), specifically visual-focussed Large Language Models (LLM).







Figure 1: In this subway sequence, Wally (Pryor) performs “simulated sight”, using memorized cues to mask his blindness.








Figure 2: During the job interview, Wally and Dave attempt to communicate across a complete sensory disconnect.




The joke, as these things go, has aged rather well. Silicon Valley has spent the better part of a decade equipping AI with eyes. Visual encoders. Camera inputs. The image-upload button is presented to us with confidence that the machine can now see. What the product announcements rarely discuss is the architecture sitting behind the lens. The LLMs process visual information by first converting it into words; then reasoning about those words; and, finally describing what they believe to be there. All with the practiced confidence of a man who cannot see the bar fight he has just walked into.
The Wally Problem
Silicon Valley’s flagship general-purpose LLMs still have the language bottleneck firmly in place. The chatbot works, ostensibly, because the partnership is all it has. This appears to be a Wally problem. Vision for most multimodal AI systems relies on a process of narration, not perception. Pixels enter; the language model converts them into tokens; the tokens are then reasoned about (Su et al., 2025). Under light cognitive load, this works well enough. Under heavier demands requiring genuine inference, the visual attention collapses, and the model does what researchers have delicately termed “relying on linguistic priors” (Qian et al., 2026). It does a Wally. It narrates the world it expects rather than the one in front of it. In other words, it does not merely struggle to see. It hallucinates with pre-trained confidence.

Qian, Z., Ma, Y., Ouyang, Z., Wang, Z., Xu, Z., Luo, F., Liu, X., Ge, Z., Guo, Y., & Han, J. (2026). Cognitive pivot points and visual anchoring: Unveiling and rectifying hallucinations in multimodal reasoning models. arXiv Preprint arXiv:2604.10219. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10219
But what about Tesla?
An instinctive counter-argument could be to point to Tesla. If the LLM cannot see, how then is a two-tonne vehicle able to negotiate Californian roads without incident? The answer is not that Tesla has solved the vision problem. The Tesla v12 architecture maps pixels directly to steering and braking outputs, bypassing language altogether. There is no Dave whispering directions to Wally here. The blind man has simply been removed. The car does not name a stop sign before responding to it; it encodes the sign as a spatial object with associated coordinates and probabilities, and acts accordingly.
And Midjourney?
Another apparent aesthetic counter-argument are the many visual generation tools of which Midjourney is the prime example. The remarkable images these generative models produce seem to have mastered the disconnect. The light behaves. The geometry holds. The shadows fall where shadows ought to fall. One is almost persuaded. One is reminded of Wally discovering, late in the film, that he has become a rather convincing actor. Which is not the same thing as having recovered his sight. What Midjourney has mastered is the aesthetics of plausibility (Su et al., 2025). Through heroic quantities of human feedback, it has learned the statistical grammar of what beautiful images look like. It has learnt the precise pixel distribution that human evaluators label as “a convincing glass of wine” or “a plausible city at night”. It does not know that glass shatters, nor that wine is liquid. It is navigating a latent mapping of human visual taste.

Zhou, Y., Wang, Y., He, X., Xiao, R., Li, Z., Feng, Q., Guo, Z., Yang, Y., Wu, H., Huang, W., Wei, J., Si, D., Yao, X., Bu, J., Huang, H., Fu, T., Tang, S., Fei, B., Zhou, D., … Bai, L. (2025). Scientists’ first exam: Probing cognitive abilities of MLLM via perception, understanding, and reasoning. arXiv Preprint arXiv:2506.10521. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10521
The results are often beautiful, yet in the scientific domain where spatial truth crucial, completely unpredictable. When researchers recently evaluated leading multimodal models on scientific tasks requiring perception, interpretation, and reasoning over real data, performance was strikingly limited. The models achieved only around 30% accuracy, revealing substantial gaps in their ability to integrate visual information with scientific reasoning (Zhou et al., 2025).
The perception may be absent, but the vocabulary remains intact. Wally, as it turns out, knows all the right words for a bar fight.
These failures are not just academic. They are alarming. Engineers developing collaborative tools for blind and low-vision users have discovered that AI-mediated visual description collapses on the very information those users most need: spatial structure (Li et al., 2026). Where is the annotation relative to the diagram? Which cluster corresponds to which label? The visual grammar of arrangement and proximity as semantic signal evaporates in translation. A system that cannot genuinely parse space cannot reconstruct it for the people whose relationship to space is already precarious. Asking Wally to give directions, in other words, has consequences that extend well beyond comedy.

Li, M., Yang, H., Sanda, N., & Das, M. (2026). Idea11y: Enhancing accessibility in collaborative ideation for blind or low vision screen reader users. Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3790878

Su, Z., Xia, P., Guo, H., Liu, Z., Ma, Y., Qu, X., Liu, J., Li, Y., Zeng, K., Yang, Z., Li, L., Cheng, Y., Ji, H., He, J., & Fung, Y. R. (2025). Thinking with images for multimodal reasoning: Foundations, methods, and future frontiers. arXiv Preprint arXiv:2506.23918. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23918
The field is not entirely unaware of the predicament. A growing body of research advocates for what its proponents call “thinking with images” rather than thinking about them. In other words, reasoning natively in visual latent space, rather than routing every observation through the linguistic bottleneck first (Su et al., 2025). Whether this amounts to a genuine architectural reckoning or a more sophisticated performance of sight is, for now, an open question.
The partnership of Wally and Dave, for the moment, endures. Wally strides forward; Dave shouts what he thinks he lip-read. The demos are polished. The press releases are stirring. The benchmarks, carefully selected, are excellent.
The bar fight, however, is still going on. And it is becoming increasingly difficult for us as outsiders to tell which punches are actually landing with great conviction and which ones are striking empty air.

It’s also doing a Dave.
The visual encoder is Wally — performing sight, converting what it sees into the expected answer. The language model is Dave — filling the gaps with linguistic priors, delivering direction based on what it thinks it understood.
Wally and Dave. Running simultaneously. In every multimodal AI system you are currently using.
The camera input is real. The confidence is real. The sight — and the hearing — are not.
[click]

title: The Spotted Ape
text:
AI narrates theworld it expects— not the onein front of it.


[Slower. This is the thesis. Give the room time to hold it.]
Silicon Valley has spent a decade equipping AI with eyes. Visual encoders. Image inputs. The image-upload button arrives with the confidence of a product announcement.
What the press releases don’t discuss is the architecture behind the lens.
Pixels come in. They are converted to words. The words are reasoned about. And then the system tells you — with complete confidence — what it expects to be there.
That is Wally on the subway. Asserting “I’m not white” — not because he’s seen himself, but because it’s the answer his training gives him.
Dave, meanwhile, is shouting directions.
[click]

title: The Spotted Ape
The Spotted Ape
The Spotted Ape
text:
Mastering Beauty,Missing Meaning


I can hear you. What about Midjourney? The light behaves. The geometry holds. The shadows fall exactly where they ought to fall.
Wally, late in the film, discovers he has become a rather convincing actor.
Which is not the same thing as having recovered his sight.
[click]

title: The Spotted Ape
text:
30%


<div class="stat-eyebrow">The Perception Gap</div>
<div class="stat-desc">Accuracy rate for leading multimodal models on scientific visual reasoning tasks. Not aesthetic plausibility — genuine sight.</div>
<div class="stat-kicker">The vocabulary is intact. The perception is absent.</div>



The Spotted Ape  ·  Design Strategy


Thirty percent.
[pause — full count of three]
That is the accuracy rate when leading multimodal models face scientific tasks requiring actual visual reasoning. Not aesthetic plausibility.
Genuine sight.
Thirty percent.
The vocabulary is intact. The perception is absent. Wally knows all the right words for a bar fight.
[click]

title: The Spotted Ape
text:
Spatial TruthCollapses


[Quieter now. This is where it stops being a technical argument.]
Engineers building tools for blind and low-vision users have found that AI-mediated visual description collapses precisely on the information those users need most.
Not the general subject. The spatial structure. Where is this element relative to that one? What is the relationship between these two things?
The visual grammar of arrangement — proximity as meaning — evaporates in translation.
[pause]
Asking Wally for directions has consequences that extend well beyond the comedy.
His performance of sight, when trusted, causes real harm.
[click]

title: The Spotted Ape
The Spotted Ape
text:
This is not anAI problem. It is a designproblem.


[Step back. This is the pivot. It is aimed directly at the people in this room.]
Here is the thing about Wally and Dave.
They didn’t write their own script. Someone handed it to them.
[pause]
Designers are supposed to be the people in this process who can actually see. Who bring proximity, lived experience, and genuine contextual judgment. That is the job. That is what separates design from decoration.
What is happening instead — in teams and organisations running this at scale every day — is this: designers are loading AI systems with assumptions they already hold. Briefs built from abstraction. Research that confirms what was expected. Insights that have been translated through language before they were ever tested against reality.
Then treating the output as direction.
[pause]
The AI cannot see what it hasn’t been given. It performs confidence with whatever it receives. That is its nature.
But the designer is not the architecture. The designer is the shepherd.
And a shepherd who hands the flock to Wally and Dave — and then follows their lead — has not solved anything.
They have simply moved the blindness upstream. And made it invisible.
[pause]
The AI is the clearest mirror the design industry currently has.
What it reflects is not a technology problem.
It reflects an industry that handed the eyes to something blind — and called it a methodology.
[click]

title: The Spotted Ape
text:
Stop Narrating.Start Perceiving.


Read the full essay at  spottedape.substack.com


Three things. Not ten.
[pause]
Reason natively in context. Don’t translate lived experience into abstraction before acting on it. Proximity changes what you are capable of seeing — not just how you feel about the process.
[pause]
Proximity is a design method. Not a values statement. A structural commitment — to building teams and processes genuinely close to the problem before solutions begin.
[pause]
Design with, not for. The gap between those two words is exactly where products fail the people who need them most. Knowing the gap exists, and performing across it anyway — that is the Wally move.
[pause — settle — make eye contact]
Wally strides forward. Dave shouts what he thinks he lip-reads.
The demos are polished. The benchmarks, carefully selected, are excellent.
But the bar fight is still going on.
And it is becoming increasingly difficult, as outsiders, to tell which punches are landing — and which ones are striking empty air.
[Stop. Say nothing more.]
Thank you.

Ethical AI integration
Identity formation
Translating AI fluency into employability

Variable access to hardware
Psychological resistance to AI

The recent viral clip, shared by Harry Shimmin, mirrors the seismic upheaval generative AI is bringing to the design space. What began as a distant hum—tools quietly assisting with iterations—has surged into a transformative force, reshaping how ideas are conceived, refined, and executed.
When I first tried chatGPT with MidJourney and DALL-E 3, I realised an avalanche was coming. It took a concept I’d been stuck on for weeks and turned it into something real. AI as a creative tool is pushing us past our limits. ChatGPTo1 is here. Cursor, Replit, and 3D AI are knocking on the door. The AI agents aren’t just beckoning. They’re pulling up chairs at the table. Will AI eat the world? Maybe not all at once, but it sure looks hungry.
Prototyping the Future: AI as a Catalyst for Innovation
In the creative design field, the iterative process has long been constrained by time and resources. AI obliterates those limits. Tools like Midjourney, Magnific AI, Runway and MiniMax‘s HailuoAI now allow designers to test dozens of visual ideas in hours rather than weeks. The ability to render photorealistic product concepts or conceptual ad campaigns in real time compresses timelines and broadens possibilities.
Yet, it’s more than just speed. Accenture reports companies that successfully integrate AI into innovation processes achieve up to 15% greater revenue performance than their peers, with that margin set to more than double by 2026. In creative design, this could mean agencies that embrace AI not only deliver faster but develop work that connects more deeply with audiences.
Consider the rise of hyper-personalised content. AI-powered algorithms can tailor designs to individual preferences at scale, creating bespoke customer experiences. For example, a fashion brand might use generative AI to design personalised marketing campaigns as pioneered by Klarna, adapting not only the message but the aesthetic to align with a recipient’s tastes and buying history.

Creativity Augmented, Not Replaced
A perennial fear in the design world is that AI might supplant human ingenuity. But as the Creative Trends Report 2025 of Adobe suggests, the reality is far more collaborative. AI is emerging as a co-creator, amplifying human potential rather than replacing it.
For designers, an example of the new workflows looks like this: start with a loose concept, use AI to generate a spectrum of iterations, then apply human intuition to refine and align the results with a specific vision or brand ethos. It’s the difference between sketching a dozen ideas yourself and having a tool suggest hundreds, freeing the designer to focus on selection and aesthetic finishing.
This dynamic partnership goes beyond efficiency. It encourages designers to explore ideas previously deemed too abstract or unfeasible. By removing the technical and financial constraints of traditional prototyping, AI enables creative risks that might have been discarded at the brainstorming stage.

The Skills Avalanche: Preparing for the Shift
With these opportunities comes a demand for new expertise. Creative professionals who once focused solely on aesthetics or messaging must now learn to interface with technology. Bain & Company’s research report highlights the growing importance of hybrid roles that include:

Prompt Engineers: Experts in crafting precise AI instructions to achieve desired design outputs.
Data Storytellers: Professionals who translate AI-driven insights into compelling narratives for campaigns.

The shift requires not just new skills but a new mindset—one that sees AI as a creative partner rather than a competitor. Forward-looking agencies and firms are already investing in training programs to bridge this gap, ensuring their teams remain agile in an AI-driven world.

Ethics in Design: Creativity Meets Responsibility
The creative design space sits at the crossroads of opportunity and risk. As AI generates breathtakingly realistic visuals and compelling narratives, the potential for misuse grows. From deepfake content to algorithmic bias, the risks to trust and integrity in design are significant.
Kantar Media‘s 2025 Media Trends and Predictions highlights a key concern: users are demanding transparency about how AI tools shape what they see. For designers, this means developing clear frameworks around content ownership, disclosure of AI’s role in creation, and safeguarding against manipulation.
Agencies must internalize the legal and ethical implications of AI-driven creativity. This isn’t about ticking boxes or setting up bureaucratic committees—it’s about embedding a culture of responsibility into every stage of the creative process. Designers and strategists need to ask hard questions: Who owns the content? How do we ensure fairness? What happens if AI makes a decision we can’t explain?
The answers won’t come from more paperwork but from a mindset shift—treating ethical considerations as integral to design, not an afterthought. Brands thrive on trust, and in an AI-powered world, trust isn’t won by accident.

Reimagining Strategy: The Designer’s Role in an AI-Driven World
The influx of AI tools isn’t just a technological revolution; it’s a cultural one. The role of a designer is shifting from executor to orchestrator—someone who leverages AI to imagine new possibilities, then crafts the connective tissue that makes those ideas resonate.
Real-time market insights powered by generative AI are changing the way creative teams approach campaigns. No longer static, strategies evolve dynamically based on continuous feedback from AI models. This adaptability is a game-changer, enabling brands to stay ahead in rapidly shifting markets.
But success demands more than technological fluency. Designers must remain the guardians of empathy and authenticity, ensuring AI outputs reflect the human values that make great design timeless.
Just as Harry Shimmin in Kyrgyzstan escaped the avalanche by correctly estimating its momentum. For designers, it’s like finding out your competition isn’t just faster—it’s tireless, omnipresent, and suspiciously good at brainstorming at 3 a.m. You can’t out-sketch it, out-code it, or outlast it. The avalanche is here. Ride it, or hope your bunker holds.
After all, if software ate the world, AI seems ready for dessert.

Is generative AI the end of creativity? Not at all. Designers are now swimming alongside AI—not being replaced but gaining a powerful ally, for now. According to MIT’s recent study, Artificial Intelligence, Scientific Discovery, and Product Innovation by Aidan Toner-Rodgers, AI is a transformative partner reshaping R&D. Here’s a breakdown of key insights and their implications for designers:

More Innovation: Scientists using AI discovered 44% more novel materials, leading to a 39% rise in patent filings and a 17% boost in prototypes. For designers, this could mean faster ideation and exploration of creative possibilities.
More Novel Ideas: AI-driven discoveries introduced unique innovations instead of mere upgrades. This suggests that AI has the potential to push designers beyond simple refinements, opening entirely new avenues in form, function, and concept.
Unequal Benefits: Only the most productive scientists saw significant gains, while others benefited less. This insight implies that designers who excel at developing and filtering ideas are best positioned to leverage AI effectively.
Evaluation is Key: While AI generates more ideas, scientists spent extra time determining which were valuable. Designers may likewise need to sharpen their “curation” skills to select the most promising AI-generated designs.
Expertise Matters: Scientists with strong judgement skills thrived, focusing on promising ideas and ignoring noise. For designers, AI doesn’t replace expertise—it makes it even more crucial. Those who can discern quality in AI’s flood of options will excel.
Productivity vs. Satisfaction: Despite increased productivity, many scientists reported feeling less satisfied, sensing that their creativity was underutilised. This emphasises that designers should develop AI tools that truly complement their creative strengths, rather than let AI define their process.

The Bottom Line: The best results come to those who know how to handle AI-generated ideas. Expertise and curation are essential as AI churns out concepts at unprecedented speed. The question isn’t “Will AI replace us?” but rather, “Will we adapt fast enough to co-create effectively?”
Generative AI can amplify our work—but those who excel will be the ones who turn AI’s raw output into refined creativity.

 > “It’s the end of explanations, a great increase in reality is here.” –K Allado-McDowell and GPT-3, Air Age Blueprint
AI’s integration into the field of design appears to be highlighting a profound transition from creating artefacts to working with systems that think, adapt, and influence. In K Allado-McDowell’s compelling youtube talk, Designing Neural Media, a framework emerges that challenges us to rethink our role as designers in this new era. Drawing on the legacy of visionaries like McLuhan, K’s work maps out a 30-year evolution of media that progresses from broadcast and immersive forms, through network media, and now into the realm of neural media.
Allado-McDowell proposes a cogent continuum of four media waves. First is Broadcast Media, traditional media such as radio and television employing one-to-many communication, which developed from the 1920s to the 1950s. Second is Immersive Media, which provide engaging experiences like cinema and virtual reality, spanning from the 1950s to the 1980s. Third is Network Media, encompassing the internet and social media and enabling user interaction, emerging from the 1980s to the 2010s. Fourth is Neural Media, AI-based media (i.e., generative AI and brain-computer interfaces) that are emerging from the 2010s-2020s and beyond.
Allado-McDowell argues that this latest wave is built on AI’s neural networks and hints at future integrations with brain-computer interfaces, transforming our tools from passive artefacts into dynamic, generative systems that not only respond but also learn and adapt. For modern design strategists, this shift demands we move beyond pursuing aesthetic excellence and conventional problem-solving; instead, we are now tasked with architecting intelligence itself. The challenge lies in creating systems that think, adapt, and ultimately influence human cognition, thereby fundamentally reshaping our approach to design.
Central to Allado-McDowell’s argument is the notion that we are at an early, malleable stage in the development of neural media. We are at a pivotal moment when design choices can shape cultural identity, ethical norms, and even political structures. Designing neural media, therefore, involves developing a critical literacy to understand AI’s capabilities, limitations, and underlying biases. It calls for experimentation (i.e., engaging in co-creation projects with AI) which can reveal entirely new modes of artistic expression and subjectivity. Moreover, by actively engaging with these emerging technologies, designers and creators can promote values like inclusivity, creativity, and democratic subject formation, whilst mitigating risks such as bias, manipulation, and loss of privacy. Allado-McDowell compares this process to guiding the growth of a tree, where early interventions in the structure of neural media can profoundly affect how we come to understand ourselves and our relationship with technology.
Embracing neural media compels us to integrate ethical considerations, cultural context, and systems thinking into our work. It is about designing for an interconnected future in which our creations actively shape and redefine the human experience. Allado-McDowell’s insights suggest that deep engagement with these emerging technologies is essential to building a future where design and intelligent systems co-evolve for the betterment of society. Interesting talk. Thank you K Allado-McDowell.

Klarna, the Swedish payments giant, has taken a revolutionary approach to its marketing strategy by handing over complete control of 30 campaigns across 45 countries to generative AI. This bold experiment not only demonstrated the creative potential of AI but also showcased its ability to deliver significant business impact.
Traditionally, large-scale campaigns require vast resources for localised imagery, nuanced translations, and culturally resonant content. Klarna’s AI-driven campaigns streamlined this process dramatically. Tools like MidJourney and Firefly were employed to create visuals, replacing traditional production pipelines and eliminating the need for stock imagery. These innovations reduced the production cycle from six weeks to just seven days while ensuring high-quality, brand-aligned content.

“Historically, we had to pay an agency or an artist to bring these ideas to life. We’ve saved millions on that ideation process alone,” Klarna’s CMO, David Sandstrom, said.

The results speak volumes. Marketing costs were slashed by 11% in Q1 2024, amounting to approximately $10 million in savings. This includes a $6 million reduction in image production costs and $4 million saved on external suppliers for tasks like translations and CRM management. Beyond cost savings, the AI campaigns delivered outstanding engagement metrics, with some email click-through rates surging by up to 400%.
This strategy allowed the company to scale personalised marketing for events such as Mother’s Day and Black Friday without the logistical bottlenecks of traditional workflows. AI didn’t just match human-created campaigns in quality—it often surpassed them in both creativity and performance.
This experiment underscores a pivotal moment in designing marketing strategies: generative AI isn’t just a brutally efficient cost-cutting tool but a driver of innovation and growth, redefining how brands connect with their audiences. The ability to maintain brand integrity while scaling creative output could nudge other brands to rethink their marketing strategies, proving that AI has moved from being an experiment to a competitive necessity. The challenge now is ensuring these innovations remain rooted in the human-centred principles that underpin great design.
Is your brand ready to embrace AI as a co-creator?

User Experience (UX) expert Greg Nudelman recently published a provocative piece arguing that the collaborative web application Figma “is the Titanic that is about to hit that new UX iceberg at full speed and sink” (Nudelman, 2025). His research, along with supporting academic work, provides compelling evidence that this isn’t just hyperbole.
The Great Interface Flip
Nielsen Norman Group identifies AI as “the first new User Interface (UI) paradigm in 60 years,” moving us from command-based interaction to intent-based outcome specification (Nielsen Norman Group, 2023). The implications are profound.

The “Iceberg UX Model” (Nudelman, 2025)
Nudelman (2025) introduces the “Iceberg UX Model”. Traditionally, UI was the bulk of the user experience, like an inverted pyramid. But AI-first systems are flipping this upside down. The UI becomes just “that teeny tiny little triangle on top” while the real experience happens beneath: data processing, automation logic, and intelligent decision-making.
Why Traditional Design Tools Are Struggling
The research reveals a fundamental mismatch. In AI-first applications, “the actual UI is simply not that important to the customer,” echoing Alan Cooper’s early critique of flashy, performative interfaces that hinder more than they help (Cooper, 1999).
Take any AI document summariser, as Nudelman (2025) points out. Background colour? “Nope. Not a chance.” Font sizes? “Don’t make me laugh.” What matters is “the length of the content, the organisation of the summary, its completeness, accuracy, reliability, readability, and scannability.”
None of these critical UX elements can be properly expressed in Figma.
The Skills Gap Widens
The academic research analysing 43 sources across industry and academia (Maré, 2025) found that 95% of a UX designer’s contribution should now focus on: use case validation, AI model research, data flow workshops, understanding AI decision matrices, and customer problem-solving.
UI design? “Probably 5% is the actual UI design” (Nudelman, 2025).
The Path Forward
The path forward isn’t about Figma being replaced by AI. It is rather about the UI itself becoming less central to user experience. Companies like IBM are already moving toward design systems as code (IBM, 2025), while conversational interfaces minimise the need for traditional visual design.
The designers thriving in this shift are those who’ve evolved from “pixel pushers” to experience designers in the true sense of the word, that focus on how AI models behave, what data flows through systems, and how to validate real user problems.
The Bottom Line
As Nudelman (2025) puts it: “If you, as a UX designer, are seen as somebody who is continuously slowing down the release process in favor of adding decoration, instead of speeding up and streamlining delivery of value, you are going to be seen as a bottleneck and your position will be eliminated.”
The question isn’t whether Figma will adapt (they’re certainly trying with recent AI features). It’s whether the entire premise of visual-first design tools remains relevant when the interface itself is disappearing.
Pertinent to this dilemma is the recent launch of Jonathan Ive’s io: a collaboration between LoveFrom and OpenAI. Key to the collaboration is the recognition that the interface is dissolving and that we need a new set of tools. Strapping jet engines to old chariots is bound to fail.
Sam Altman and Jony Ive present their collaboration (OpenAI, 2025).

Are you seeing this shift in your own work? How are you adapting your design practice for AI-first systems?
